deep.reconstruction:
Folio 9r contains no mathematics: no formulas, derivations or computations. It is a continuous page of the historical introduction (Section 1) of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Ueber die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (written 1854, published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867). This sheet appears to be a fair copy.

The left-margin line 'et la propagation du son.' ends the footnote title begun on the previous page. That footnote cites Lagrange's 'Recherches sur la nature et la propagation du son' (Misc. Taur. I, 1759).

The main text continues the sentence from the previous page. Lagrange tried to determine the vibrations of a weightless string loaded with an undetermined number n of equal masses at equal spacing. He then examined how these vibrations change as n tends to infinity.

In modern terms (my gloss, not written on the page), the discrete problem is m y_k'' = (T/h)(y_{k+1} - 2y_k + y_{k-1}), with y_0 = y_{n+1} = 0. Its normal modes are y_k ∝ sin(jkπ/(n+1)) cos(ω_j t), with ω_j = 2 sqrt(T/(m h)) sin(jπ/(2(n+1))). The previous page's finite sine-interpolation formula rests on the discrete orthogonality of these sine vectors.

Riemann judges the first, finite part of the work skilful and acute. He says the passage from the finite to the infinite 'left much to be desired'. As a result, d'Alembert, in the memoir opening his Opuscules mathématiques (Tome I, 1761), could keep claiming the greatest generality for his own solution y = φ(x+t) + ψ(x−t). The leading mathematicians stayed divided, and each kept his position in later work.

Riemann then summarises the three views:
- Euler introduced arbitrary functions into analysis and, relying on geometric intuition, applied the infinitesimal calculus to them.
- Lagrange (Misc. Taur. II, p. 18) accepted Euler's results, namely his geometric construction of the course of the vibration. He was not satisfied with Euler's geometric treatment of these functions.
- D'Alembert (Opuscules I, 1761, p. 16, arts. VII–XX) accepted Euler's way of conceiving the matter. The sentence continues on the next page: he confined himself to contesting Euler's results because for arbitrary functions one cannot know whether their derivatives are continuous.
errors: No mathematical errors: the page contains no mathematics.

Historically, Riemann's summary is the standard (and broadly accurate) account of the vibrating-string controversy. Saying Lagrange's limit passage 'left much to be desired' is an evaluative judgment shared by later historians (e.g. Burkhardt, Truesdell).

results.what: Historical account of Lagrange's beaded-string approach (finite n masses, then n→∞) and its unsatisfactory limit passage
results.modern_name: Discrete-to-continuum limit of the loaded string; history of the vibrating-string controversy
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange 1759 (problem); historiographic summary by Riemann 1854/1867, later Burkhardt 1908 and Truesdell 1960

results.what: Characterisation of the positions of Euler, Lagrange and d'Alembert on arbitrary functions and on representability by trigonometric series
results.modern_name: Eighteenth-century function-concept debate (Euler vs d'Alembert vs Lagrange vs D. Bernoulli)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a page of the well-known published historical introduction to Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift on trigonometric series. It contains no mathematics, and its content has been in print since 1867.

checkable.asserts: Discrete sine orthogonality (sum is 0 for i≠j), which underlies Lagrange's finite interpolation formula discussed on the previous page (context, not written on this page).
The normalisation: the sum of sin^2 equals (n+1)/2, so the expression is 0 (context).

The sine vectors are eigenvectors of the beaded-string difference operator with eigenvalue -4 sin^2(jπ/(2(n+1))), giving Lagrange's normal modes (modern gloss, not on page); the expression simplifies to 0.
d'Alembert's general solution satisfies the wave equation y_tt = y_xx (context for 'his solution'); the result is 0.

transcription_corrections: The left-margin 'et la propagation du son.' continues the footnote from the previous page, citing Lagrange, 'Recherches sur la nature et la propagation du son', Misc. Taur. I. It is not part of the body text.

Near the end the transcription reads 'Auffassungsweise der Differentialrechnung'. The published text, as I recall it, has 'Auffassungsweise der Differentialgleichung'. The handwriting is ambiguous, so this should be checked against the image.
Otherwise the machine transcription agrees closely with the image. Modern spelling ('willkürlichen', 'größten') stands for Riemann's 'willkührlichen' and long-s/ß forms.
